concepts.title: Backward Mapping
concepts.one_liner: Backward mapping loops over target image pixels and applies an inverse geometric transform to find corresponding values in the input image, ensuring no missing values.
concepts.content:
(see figure: Comparison between forward and backward mapping using nearest neighbor interpolation. Forward mapping will produce missing values.)

The best approach for image warping is to use backward mapping, which consists of looping over all the pixels of the target image and applying the inverse geometric transform, $\mathbf{M}^{-1}$. Interpolation is then used to determine the correct color value from the input image. This process guarantees that there will be no missing values, unless the coordinates fall outside the frame of the input image, and eliminates aliasing if interpolation is performed correctly. To avoid aliasing when the target image has a lower pixel density than the input image, blurring the input image might be necessary. Figures (Figure 1.1.6) and (Figure 1.1.7) compare forward and backward mapping.

(see figure: Comparison between forward and backward mapping. Forward mapping produces many artifacts. In both cases we use nearest neighbor interpolation.)
concepts.motivation_md: Forward mapping often results in "holes" or missing values in the target image because multiple input pixels might map to the same output pixel while others are skipped. Backward mapping solves this by ensuring every pixel in the target grid is assigned a value.
concepts.recap_md: - Loop over target pixels and apply the inverse transformation $\mathbf{M}^{-1}$ to find source coordinates.

concepts.title: MIP-mapping
concepts.one_liner: MIP-mapping is a technique for high-quality interpolation that uses a multiscale image pyramid to efficiently determine the best neighborhood structure for warping.
concepts.content: MIP-mapping is a popular technique for high quality and efficient interpolation. It relies on a multiscale image pyramid to efficiently compute the best neighborhood structure needed to perform the interpolation at each location. This approach is particularly useful when warping an image onto a curved surface.
concepts.motivation_md: Standard interpolation can be computationally expensive or produce aliasing when scaling images significantly. MIP-mapping provides a pre-computed multiscale structure to make this process faster and smoother.

concepts.title: Implicit Image Representation
concepts.one_liner: An implicit image representation uses a trained function $f_\theta$ to map continuous coordinates $(x,y)$ to image values.
concepts.content:
An image is typically an array of values, $\boldsymbol\ell\in \mathbb{R}^{N \times M \times 3}$, where each value is indexed as $\ell[n,m]$ for discrete values of $n$ and $m$. Interpolation can be viewed as a way of transforming this discrete image into a continuous signal $\ell(x,y)$.

An implicit image representation via a function $f_\theta$ trained to reproduce the image pixels is a function such that:
$$\ell(x,y) = f_{\theta}(x,y)$$
In this representation, $x$ and $y$ can take on any real value.
concepts.motivation_md: Representing images as continuous functions rather than discrete grids allows for infinite resolution and easier geometric transformations without standard interpolation artifacts.
concepts.recap_md: - Transforms discrete pixel arrays into a continuous signal $\ell(x,y)$.

concepts.title: Image Warping with Implicit Representations
concepts.one_liner: Image warping with implicit representations applies an inverse geometric transformation to output grid coordinates and queries a neural network for values.
concepts.content:
Once a neural network $f_{\theta}(x,y)$ has learned to reproduce an image, it can be used to reconstruct the original or apply transformations. Image warping is implemented by applying the inverse geometric transformation to the discrete coordinates of the output grid and using the functional representation of the image to obtain interpolated values:
$$\hat{\ell} (x,y) = f_{\theta} \left( \mathbf{M}^{-1}(x,y,1)^\mathsf{T}\right)$$
In this formulation, the input location is written in homogeneous coordinates; the function $f$ must divide by the third component to translate the input back to heterogeneous coordinates before processing.
concepts.motivation_md: By using a learned continuous function, warping becomes a simple matter of coordinate transformation and function evaluation, avoiding the need for manual interpolation kernels.
concepts.recap_md: - Apply $\mathbf{M}^{-1}$ to target coordinates and pass the result to the learned function $f_\theta$.

concepts.title: Image Alignment
concepts.one_liner: Image alignment is the process of identifying the transformation $\mathbf{M}$ that relates two images.
concepts.content: Image alignment is the reverse problem of image warping. Given two images where one is a transformed version of the other, the goal is to identify the specific transformation $\mathbf{M}$ that relates them.
concepts.motivation_md: Alignment is crucial for tasks like image stitching (panoramas), medical imaging registration, and motion tracking, where the relationship between different views must be quantified.
concepts.recap_md: - The goal is to find the transformation matrix $\mathbf{M}$ between two images.

concepts.title: Spatial Transformer Network
concepts.one_liner: A spatial transformer network uses parametric image transformations within a neural network to align training examples into a canonical pose.
concepts.content: The spatial transformer network is an example of using parametric image transformations inside a neural network. Such transformations can be helpful during the learning process to align training examples into a canonical pose, making it easier for the network to process them.
concepts.motivation_md: Neural networks often struggle with spatial invariance; spatial transformers allow a network to actively warp input data to a standard orientation, improving classification or detection performance.

concepts.title: 2D Translation
concepts.one_liner: Translation by a 2D vector shifts coordinates by adding an offset, which can be represented as a matrix product in homogeneous coordinates.
concepts.content:
Consider a translation by a 2D vector $(t_x, t_y)$ as shown in (see figure: (left) Translation. (right) Composition of two consecutive translations.). In heterogeneous coordinates, the transformation is an addition:
$$\begin{pmatrix} x' \\ y' \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} x \\ y \end{pmatrix} + \begin{pmatrix} t_x \\ t_y \end{pmatrix}$$

This translation can be written in homogeneous coordinates as a matrix product:
$$\begin{bmatrix} x' \\ y' \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & t_x \\ 0 & 1 & t_y \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$$

This transforms an addition into a product by a matrix $\mathbf{T}$ and a vector $\mathbf{p}$, such that $\mathbf{p}' = \mathbf{T} \mathbf{p}$. In homogeneous coordinates, both matrices and vectors are defined up to a non-zero multiplicative scaling factor.

To cascade two translation operations $\mathbf{t}$ and $\mathbf{s}$ in heterogeneous coordinates, we have $\mathbf{p}' = \mathbf{p} + \mathbf{t} + \mathbf{s}$. In homogeneous coordinates, we cascade the corresponding translation matrices: $\mathbf{p}' = \mathbf{S} \mathbf{T} \mathbf{p}$. Chaining translations is performed by multiplying the matrices together:
$$\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & t_x \\ 0 & 1 & t_y \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & s_x \\ 0 & 1 & s_y \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & t_x+s_x \\ 0 & 1 & t_y+s_y \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$$
concepts.motivation_md: In standard 2D coordinates, translation is an addition operation, while rotation and scaling are multiplications. By using homogeneous coordinates, translation becomes a matrix multiplication, allowing all geometric transformations to be treated uniformly and combined through simple matrix composition.

concepts.title: 2D Scaling
concepts.one_liner: Scaling transforms the $x$ and $y$ axes by factors $s_x$ and $s_y$ using a diagonal matrix in homogeneous coordinates.
concepts.content:
Scaling the $x$-axis by $s_x$ and the $y$-axis by $s_y$ yields the transformation matrix in homogeneous coordinates:
$$\mathbf{S} = \begin{bmatrix} s_x & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & s_y & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$$

The scaling matrix is a diagonal matrix. (see figure: Non-uniform or anisotropic scaling. In this example the $y$-axis is compressed and the $x$-axis is expanded.)

Uniform scaling is obtained when $s_x=s_y$, otherwise the scaling is nonuniform or anisotropic. After uniform scaling, all angles are preserved. In all cases, parallel lines remain parallel. Areas are scaled by the determinant of the scaling matrix.
concepts.motivation_md: Scaling is used to change the size of objects or to stretch them along specific axes. Representing it as a matrix allows it to be easily combined with rotations and translations in a single transformation pipeline.
concepts.recap_md: - Scaling is represented by a diagonal matrix where the diagonal elements are the scale factors.

concepts.title: 2D Rotation
concepts.one_liner: Rotation by an angle $\theta$ is represented by an orthogonal matrix in homogeneous coordinates that preserves distances to the origin.
concepts.content:
For a rotation by an angle $\theta$, the matrix in homogeneous coordinates is:
$$\mathbf{R} = \begin{bmatrix} \cos(\theta) & \sin(\theta) & 0 \\ -\sin(\theta) & \cos(\theta) & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$$

(see figure: Rotation by an angle $\theta$ counterclockwise around the origin.)

A rotation in homogeneous coordinates is a product $\mathbf{p}' = \mathbf{R} \mathbf{p}$. Chaining two rotations with angles $\alpha$ and $\beta$ is equivalent to applying a single rotation with angle $\alpha+\beta$. The determinant of a rotation matrix is 1 and the matrix is orthogonal, meaning $\mathbf{R}^\mathsf{T}= \mathbf{R}^{-1}$. The distance between any point and the origin does not change after a rotation.

In heterogeneous coordinates, the transformation uses only the upper-left $2\times2$ matrix. While homogeneous coordinates offer no direct benefit for rotation alone, they allow rotation and translation to be combined as products of matrices. For very small angles, the rotation matrix can be approximated by its Taylor development:
$$\mathbf{R} \simeq \begin{bmatrix} 1 & \theta & 0 \\ -\theta & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$$

For small angles, a rotation becomes a shear. In general, a rotation can be written as two shears and a scaling.
concepts.motivation_md: Rotations are fundamental for changing the orientation of objects. By representing them as matrices, we can use linear algebra to calculate new positions and combine rotations with other transformations like translation.
concepts.recap_md: - Rotation matrices are orthogonal, meaning their transpose is their inverse.

key_passage.text: For a rotation by an angle θ, we simply have the matrix in homogeneous coordinates: a rotation in homogeneous coordinates is a product p' = R p.

motivation.text: The advantage is that now both rotation and translation are written in the same way! They are both products of a matrix times a vector, so that they can be combined as we will discuss in sec-chaining_transformations.

concepts.title: 2D Shearing
concepts.one_liner: Shearing displaces points along one axis by an amount proportional to their coordinate on another axis, using off-diagonal matrix elements.
concepts.content:
Shearing involves scale factors in the off-diagonal matrix locations, as shown in the matrix $\mathbf{Q}$:
$$\mathbf{Q} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & q_x & 0 \\ q_y & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$$

(see figure: Three examples of shear transformation.)

In a horizontal shear ($q_x=1, q_y=0$), points are displaced along horizontal lines by a displacement proportional to the $y$ coordinate: $x'=x+q_y y$. In a shear, lines are mapped to lines and parallel lines remain parallel, but non-zero angles between lines change.
concepts.motivation_md: Shearing is used to create slant effects or to distort shapes while preserving area and parallelism. It is a basic building block of more complex affine transformations.
concepts.recap_md: - Shearing uses off-diagonal elements in the transformation matrix to create slant.

concepts.title: Chaining Transformations
concepts.one_liner: Homogeneous coordinates allow complex geometric transformations to be built by multiplying translation, rotation, scaling, and shearing matrices.
concepts.content:
Homogeneous coordinates allow using translation, rotation, scaling, and shearing as matrix multiplications. We can build complex transformations by combining these four matrices:
$$\mathbf{p}' = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & q_x & 0 \\ q_y & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} s_x & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & s_y & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} \cos(\theta) & \sin(\theta) & 0 \\ -\sin(\theta) & \cos(\theta) & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & t_x \\ 0 & 1 & t_y \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \mathbf{p}$$

(see figure: Summary of 2D geometric transformations and their formulation in homogeneous coordinates.)

Matrix multiplication is noncommutative, so the order of operations is important. For example, rotating then translating is not the same as translating then rotating. All described transformations are relative to the origin. To rotate an image around an arbitrary central location $(t_x, t_y)$, you must first translate to the origin, rotate, and then translate back:
$$\mathbf{p}' = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & t_x \\ 0 & 1 & t_y \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} \cos(\theta) & \sin(\theta) & 0 \\ -\sin(\theta) & \cos(\theta) & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & -t_x \\ 0 & 1 & -t_y \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \mathbf{p}$$
concepts.motivation_md: Chaining allows for the creation of sophisticated movements and placements by combining simple atomic transformations. It is the standard way to handle object hierarchies and coordinate system changes in computer graphics.
concepts.recap_md: - Transformations are combined through matrix multiplication, which is order-dependent.

key_passage.text: As matrix multiplication is noncommutative, the order in which operations are performed is important (i.e., it is not the same to rotate with respect to the origin and then translate, as it is to translate and then rotate). All of the geometric transformations we have described are relative to the origin. If you want to rotate an image around an arbitrary central location, then you need to first translate to put that location at the origin, then rotate and then translate back.

motivation.text: Chaining transformations in such a way is a very important tool in computer graphics and we will also use it extensively as we dive deeper into geometry.

concepts.title: Euclidean transformation
concepts.one_liner: A Euclidean transformation is the result of chaining only rotations and translations, preserving both lengths and angles.
concepts.content: When chaining rotations and translations only, we will have a euclidean transformation. In this type of transformation, lengths and angles between lines are preserved.
concepts.motivation_md: Euclidean transformations describe 'rigid body' motions where the object's shape and size do not change, only its position and orientation.

concepts.title: Affine Transformation (2D)
concepts.one_liner: An affine transformation is a 2D transformation with six degrees of freedom that preserves the parallelism of lines.
concepts.content: In general, chaining translations, scalings, rotations, and shears results in a generic matrix of the form: $$\mathbf{p}' = \begin{bmatrix} a & b & c \\ d & e & f \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \mathbf{p}$$ Any transformation with this form (6 degrees of freedom) is an affine transformation. An affine transformation has the property that parallel lines will remain parallel after the transformation; however, lengths and non-zero angles might change.
concepts.motivation_md: Affine transformations provide a unified mathematical framework for common geometric operations like translation, rotation, and scaling, ensuring that the basic structure of parallel lines is preserved during image manipulation.

concepts.title: Line Representation in Homogeneous Coordinates

position.section_title: Lines and Planes in Homogeneous Coordinates

concepts.one_liner: In homogeneous coordinates, a 2D line is represented by a vector $\boldsymbol{l}$ such that a point $\mathbf{p}$ lies on the line if their dot product is zero.
concepts.content: One interesting application of homogeneous coordinates is to use it to describe lines and planes and perform operations with them. In 2D, the equation of a line is $ax+by+c=0$, which can be written in homogeneous coordinates as $$ax+by+c=0 \rightarrow \begin{bmatrix} a & b & c \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = 0$$ In homogeneous coordinates, the equation of a line is the dot product: $$\boldsymbol{l} ^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{p} = 0$$ where $\boldsymbol{l}^\mathsf{T}= \left [a, b, c\right ]$. Therefore, a point $\mathbf{p}$ belongs to the line when $\boldsymbol{l}$ and $\mathbf{p}$ are perpendicular. This representation of the line is in homogeneous coordinates because it is scale invariant. That is, $\left [a, b, c\right ]$ is the same line as $\left [a/c, b/c, 1\right ]$. Therefore, it is also useful to describe the equation of the line with $\boldsymbol{l}^\mathsf{T}= \left [n_x, n_y, -d\right ]$ where $(n_x,n_y)$ is the normal to the line and $d$ is the distance to the origin.
concepts.motivation_md: Representing lines as vectors in homogeneous coordinates simplifies geometric computations, allowing line-point relationships to be expressed as simple linear algebra operations.

concepts.title: Line from Two Points in Homogeneous Coordinates

position.section_title: Lines and Planes in Homogeneous Coordinates

concepts.one_liner: The line passing through two points in homogeneous coordinates is given by the cross product of those points.
concepts.content: Using homogeneous coordinates makes obtaining geometric properties of points and lines very easy. Given two points $\mathbf{p}_1$ and $\mathbf{p}_2$ in homogeneous coordinates, the line that passes by both points is the cross product ((see figure: Using homogeneous coordinates to get the line that passes by two points, and to obtain the intersection of two lines. Both operations are analogous.)): $$\boldsymbol{l} = \mathbf{p}_1 \times \mathbf{p}_2$$ This is because if the line passes by both points, it has to verify that $\boldsymbol{l}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{p}_1=0$ and $\boldsymbol{l}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{p}_2=0$. That is, the vector $\mathbf{l}$ has to be perpendicular to both $\mathbf{p}_1$ and $\mathbf{p}_2$. The cross product between $\mathbf{p}_1$ and $\mathbf{p}_2$ gives a vector that is perpendicular to both.
concepts.motivation_md: Finding the line through two points is a fundamental geometric task; homogeneous coordinates turn this into a single cross-product operation, avoiding special cases for vertical lines.

concepts.one_liner: The intersection point of two lines in homogeneous coordinates is the cross product of the vectors representing the lines.

concepts.title: Forward Mapping
concepts.one_liner: Forward mapping is an image transformation technique where each pixel from the source is mapped directly to a calculated position in the target image.
concepts.content: The first algorithm that usually comes to mind when transforming an image is to take every pixel in the original image represented as $[\ell_i,x_i,y_i]$, apply the transformation, $\mathbf{M}$, to the coordinates, and record the pixel color into the resulting coordinates in the target image ((see figure: Comparison between forward and backward mapping using nearest neighbor interpolation. Forward mapping will produce missing values.)). As coordinates might result in non-integer values, we can simply round the result to the closest pixel coordinate (i.e., nearest neighbor interpolation). This algorithm is called forward mapping. concepts.title: Image Representations
concepts.one_liner: Images can be represented as ordered arrays, sets of pixels, or continuous functions, each offering distinct advantages for signal processing, geometry, or modeling priors.
concepts.content: Images can be represented in several ways, each making different aspects of information explicit. The most common representation is the **ordered array**, where images are ordered arrays of pixel values sampled on a regular spatial grid: $$\boldsymbol\ell=\left[ \begin{matrix} \ell[1,1] & \dots & \\ \vdots & \ell[n,m] & \vdots \\ & \dots & \ell[N,M] \\ \end{matrix} \right]$$ This representation simplifies signal processing operations like convolution. Alternatively, an image can be represented as a **set of pixels**: $$\left\{ [\ell_i,x_i,y_i] : i \right\}$$ where $\ell_i$ is the intensity at location $(x_i,y_i)$. This makes geometry explicit and simplifies geometric transformations. A third option is the **continuous function** representation, $\ell(x,y) = f_{\theta}(x,y)$, which is useful for making image priors explicit and handling continuous spatial variables. These representations are not mutually exclusive and can be used simultaneously depending on whether the goal is 3D geometry, visualization, or image modeling.
concepts.motivation_md: Different computer vision tasks require different data structures; while arrays are optimized for convolution, sets are better for geometric transformations, and functions allow for resolution-independent modeling.
concepts.recap_md: - Ordered arrays represent pixels on a regular grid, which is ideal for signal processing and standard computer input.

concepts.title: Set of pixels representation
concepts.one_liner: The set of pixels representation encodes an image as a collection of points with explicit color and location, simplifying geometric transformations.
concepts.content: The set of pixels representation encodes an image as a collection of points, explicitly indicating color and location: $$\left\{ [\ell_i,x_i,y_i] : i \right\}$$ where $\ell_i$ is the pixel intensity or color recorded at location $(x_i,y_i)$. This representation makes the geometry of the image explicit. It simplifies certain operations, such as geometric transformations, by allowing direct manipulation of spatial coordinates. For instance, translating an image to the right by one pixel is achieved by creating a new set of translated pixels: $\left\{ [\ell_i,x_i+1,y_i] : i \right\}$. This format is common in geometry-based computer vision and is useful for handling image geometries where points are not on a regular array.
concepts.motivation_md: By making coordinates explicit, this representation allows for easier manipulation of image geometry and supports non-grid-based spatial data essential for 3D vision.

concepts.title: Continuous function representation
concepts.one_liner: The continuous function representation models an image as a parameterized function mapping spatial locations to intensity or color values.
concepts.content: An image can be represented as a continuous function where the input is a location $(x, y)$ and the output is an intensity or color $\ell$: $$\ell(x,y) = f_{\theta}(x,y)$$ This function $f_{\theta}$ is parameterized by coefficients $\theta$, which are estimated from the original image. This representation is commonly used to make image priors more explicit. Once learned, the function $f$ can take continuous spatial variables as input, allowing the image to be evaluated at any coordinate rather than just on a fixed pixel grid.

concepts.title: Homogeneous coordinates
concepts.one_liner: Homogeneous coordinates represent $N$-dimensional vectors in $N+1$ dimensions, enabling scale-invariant point descriptions and simplifying geometric transformations.
concepts.content: Homogeneous coordinates represent a vector of length $N$ by a vector of length $N+1$. To transform from heterogeneous (Cartesian) to homogeneous coordinates, an additional coordinate, 1, is added: $$\begin{pmatrix} x \\ y \end{pmatrix} \rightarrow \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$$ Similarly for 3D: $$\begin{pmatrix} x \\ y \\ z \end{pmatrix} \rightarrow \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ z \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$$ In this system, all non-zero scalings of a homogeneous coordinate vector are equivalent: $$\begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} \equiv \begin{bmatrix} \lambda x \\ \lambda y \\ \lambda \end{bmatrix}$$ for any non-zero scalar $\lambda$. To return to the heterogeneous representation, all entries of the homogeneous vector are divided by their last dimension: $$\begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ w \end{bmatrix} \rightarrow \begin{pmatrix} x/w \\ y/w \end{pmatrix}$$ Geometrically, a point in homogeneous coordinates is scale invariant, which is closely related to perspective projection.
